newsitem.title: RUSSIA: British firms see progress in Russia, seek changes.
newsitem.headline: British firms see progress in Russia, seek changes.

text.p: British business leaders said on Friday that economic conditions in Russia for foreign investors were improving, but called on the government to make changes to investment laws and taxes to spur further progress.
Real improvements in the investment environment would be made this year, Russia's Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin told a news conference after talks with British executives.

"We have been in Russia for 20 years, and we have now reached the stage where the outlook for our Russian involvement is more positive," said Michael Porter of Natwest Markets, the investment arm of British banker Natwest.
"On the whole we are absolutely convinced that we have made the right decision to invest in Russia," said Ysbrand Kleyn, chairman of Cadbury Confectionery ZAO.
But they both called for greater clarity in Russia's murky legal and accounting procedures. Kleyn also said that changes to the tax system was a priority.
"The main problem with Russian taxes is that they are levied on turnover and not on profits, which is particularly hard when you are setting up a new company," he said.
Yasin said the Russian government was striving to create the necessary framework to attract foreign investment, which it hopes will reach $6 billion this year.
"You can all be sure of the growing efforts of the Russian government to attract foreign investment, and that these efforts will bear fruit," he told the conference.
Yasin said he was confident a new tax code would be introduced at the start of next year which would improve conditions "not only for foreign investment, but also for Russian companies."
"I think in 1997 there will be the final decision (on the tax code)," he said.
The code can only be introduced at the beginning of a year, and must be passed by the State Duma lower house of parliament.
"(The new code) will bring Russian legislation closer into line with Western legislation," Yasin said.
British Ambassador Andrew Wood called on the Russian government for "clarity, consistency and constitutionality," so that investors could be sure their investments were safe.
He also said keeping Russian inflation under control was a key issue for British business.
Russia's annual inflation rate fell to a post-reform low of 21.8 percent in 1996, and the government plans to bring it down further to about 12 percent in 1997.
Britain is the second biggest foreign investor in Russia, and over 350 British companies have permanent offices in Moscow, according to an embassy statement.
Visible trade with Russia was one third higher in 1996 that in 1995, and UK exports to Russia were over one billion stg.
